entries.1:1: After Joshua died, the Israelites asked God which tribe should lead the fight against the Canaanites first. It shows them looking to God for direction before acting.
entries.1:2: God answered that Judah should go first and promised them victory over the land. The reader sees that God gives clear guidance and backs it with his promise.
entries.1:3: Judah asked their brother tribe Simeon to fight alongside them, promising to help Simeon in return. It's a picture of tribes working together instead of going it alone.
entries.1:4: Judah attacked and God gave them victory, defeating ten thousand enemy soldiers at Bezek. The success is credited to God, not just to their military strength.
entries.1:5: They met King Adoni-zedek in battle and defeated his Canaanite and Perizzite forces. The story continues to show God handing their enemies over to them.
entries.1:6: The king ran away, but they caught him and cut off his thumbs and big toes. This was a brutal act that crippled him, common in ancient warfare.
entries.1:7: Adoni-zedek admitted he had done the same thing to seventy kings, and now it had happened to him. He was taken to Jerusalem, where he died, showing that cruel treatment often comes back on the one who does it.
entries.1:8: Judah's men attacked Jerusalem, killed its people, and burned the city. This was total warfare as practiced in that era.
entries.1:9: After that, Judah fought the Canaanites in the hills, the southern area, and the lowlands. They kept pressing the campaign into different regions.
entries.1:10: Caleb attacked the Canaanites in Hebron, formerly called Kiriath-arba, and defeated three enemy leaders there. Caleb is shown as a faithful fighter carrying out what was promised to him.
entries.1:11: From Hebron, Caleb moved on to attack the people of Debir, which used to be called Kiriath-sepher. The advance continues town by town.
entries.1:12: Caleb offered his daughter Achsah in marriage to whoever could capture Kiriath-sepher. This was a common way in that culture to reward a brave warrior.
entries.1:13: Othniel, Caleb's nephew, captured the town and so received Achsah as his wife. He becomes an important figure later in the book.
entries.1:14: On the way, Othniel urged Achsah to ask her father for a field, and she got off her donkey to speak with Caleb. It sets up her request for something valuable.
entries.1:15: Achsah asked her father for a blessing, since the land he gave her was dry, and requested springs of water. Caleb gave her both the upper and lower springs, showing a father's generosity.
entries.1:16: The Kenites, relatives of Moses' father-in-law, left the city of palms and settled among the people of Judah in the desert near Arad. It shows other groups joining Israel's life.
entries.1:17: Judah and Simeon together defeated the Canaanites in Zephath and completely destroyed the town, renaming it Hormah. The name means destruction, marking what happened there.
entries.1:18: Judah captured Gaza, Ashkelon, and Ekron along with the land around them. These were major Philistine cities on the coast.
entries.1:19: God was with Judah, and they took the hill country, but they couldn't drive out the people in the valleys because those enemies had iron chariots. Even with God's help, some obstacles proved too strong for them at that time.
entries.1:20: Hebron was given to Caleb as Moses had promised, and he drove out the three giant descendants of Anak living there. It shows a promise from long ago finally being kept.
entries.1:21: The tribe of Judah failed to remove the Jebusites from Jerusalem, so they lived there alongside the people of Benjamin. This is the first of several failures to fully clear the land.
entries.1:22: The tribes of Joseph attacked Bethel, and God was with them. Their campaign begins with God's support.
entries.1:23: They sent spies to scout out Bethel, which used to be called Luz. They wanted information before attacking.
entries.1:24: The spies saw a man leaving the town and offered to spare him if he showed them a way in. It was a bargain made in the middle of war.
entries.1:25: The man showed them the entrance, and they killed everyone in the town but let him and his family go free. They kept their promise to him.
entries.1:26: The man moved to the land of the Hittites, built a town, and named it Luz after his old home. The name stuck, the text notes.
entries.1:27: The tribe of Manasseh failed to drive out the Canaanites from several towns, including Beth-shean and Megiddo, so those people stayed in the land. This is another incomplete victory.
entries.1:28: Later, when Israel grew stronger, they forced the Canaanites to work for them but still didn't remove them. They chose advantage over full obedience.
entries.1:29: Ephraim also failed to remove the Canaanites living in Gezer, so they lived side by side. The pattern of incomplete conquest keeps repeating.
entries.1:30: Zebulun didn't drive out the people of Kitron and Nahalol either, but made them forced laborers. Again, the enemy stayed in the land.
entries.1:31: Asher failed to take several coastal towns, including Acco and Sidon, and didn't drive their people out. Their territory remained partly in enemy hands.
entries.1:32: So the people of Asher ended up living among the Canaanites instead of replacing them. The two peoples shared the land.
entries.1:33: Naphtali didn't remove the people of Beth-shemesh and Beth-anath but lived among them and forced them to work. The same compromise shows up again.
entries.1:34: The Amorites pushed the tribe of Dan back into the hills and wouldn't let them come down into the valley. Dan was squeezed out of its lowland territory.
entries.1:35: The Amorites stayed in several hill towns, but when Joseph's tribes grew stronger they forced them to work. The enemy remained but was subdued.
entries.1:36: The boundary of the Edomites ran from the slope of Akrabbim up from Sela. This verse marks the southern edge of the land being described.
entries.2:1: God's messenger reminds Israel that God kept his promise and brought them out of Egypt into the land. It means God is faithful, and he expects his people to remember what he has done.
entries.2:2: God had told them not to make deals with the people already living in the land and to tear down their altars, but they disobeyed. The question 'what have you done?' shows that disobedience has real consequences.
entries.2:3: Because Israel did not obey, God says he will not drive out those nations for them; instead those peoples and their gods will become a trap. It means ignoring God's commands lets trouble stay in your life.
entries.2:4: When the people heard this, they cried out loud in grief. It shows that God's words hit them hard and they felt the weight of what they had done.
entries.2:5: They named the place Bochim, which means 'weepers,' and offered sacrifices to the Lord there. It means their sorrow led them to turn back to God in worship.
entries.2:6: Joshua sent the people out, and each family went to take possession of its own share of the land. It marks the end of the conquest and the start of ordinary life in the land.
entries.2:7: The people stayed faithful to God during Joshua's lifetime and the lifetimes of the leaders who outlived him and had seen God's great deeds. It means faith is strengthened by remembering what God has done.
entries.2:8: Joshua, God's servant, died at the age of 110. It reminds us that even great leaders come to an end, and the people must carry on without them.
entries.2:9: They buried Joshua in the land his family had been given, in the hill country of Ephraim. It shows he was honored and laid to rest among his own people.
entries.2:10: After that whole generation died, a new generation grew up that did not know the Lord or what he had done. It means faith must be passed on, or the next generation will not know God.
entries.2:11: The Israelites did what was evil in God's sight and served the Baals, the gods of the surrounding peoples. It means they turned from the true God to false ones.
entries.2:12: They abandoned the Lord who had brought them out of Egypt and followed the gods of the nations around them, which made God angry. It means forgetting God's rescue leads people to chase worthless things.
entries.2:13: They turned away from the Lord and served Baal and the Astartes. It shows how completely they replaced the real God with idols.
entries.2:14: God's anger burned against Israel, and he let raiders and enemies around them defeat and plunder them. It means turning from God leaves you unprotected against harm.
entries.2:15: Wherever they went, God's hand was against them and things went badly, just as he had warned. It means broken promises to God bring real trouble, not just words.
entries.2:16: God raised up judges to rescue the people from those who were cruel to them. It shows God's mercy: even when his people fail, he provides a way out.
entries.2:17: But the people would not listen to their judges; they chased other gods and quickly turned from the way their ancestors had followed. It means people can be rescued and still go right back to their old ways.
entries.2:18: Whenever God gave them a judge, he was with that judge and saved them from their enemies for as long as the judge lived, because he felt sorry for their suffering. It shows God's compassion for people in pain.
entries.2:19: When a judge died, the people went back to doing even more evil than before, serving other gods and refusing to give up their stubborn ways. It means a change that only lasts while a leader is around is not a real change.
entries.2:20: God's anger burned against Israel because they had broken his agreement and refused to listen to him. It means God takes his promises seriously, and so should we.
entries.2:21: God said he would no longer drive out the nations that were still in the land when Joshua died. It means repeated disobedience can cost us the help and blessing we once had.
entries.2:22: God left those nations there to test Israel and see whether they would walk in his ways as their ancestors did. It means tests reveal whether our faith is real.
entries.2:23: So the Lord let those nations stay in the land and did not hand them over to Joshua quickly. It means God sometimes allows difficulty to remain so his people will learn to trust and obey him.
entries.3:1: God left some enemy nations in the land to test the Israelites who had never fought in a war. It means God sometimes uses hard situations to reveal what is really in our hearts.
entries.3:2: This was also to teach the new generation how to fight, since they had no battle experience. It means hard lessons can prepare people for challenges they will face later.
entries.3:3: These were the specific enemy groups still living in the land, including Philistine rulers and several Canaanite peoples. It means the pressure on Israel came from many sides at once.
entries.3:4: God used these nations to test whether Israel would obey his commands given through Moses. It means obedience is proven in real situations, not just in words.
entries.3:5: The Israelites ended up living side by side with the Canaanites and other peoples instead of removing them. It means close contact with wrong influences can slowly pull us away from what is right.
entries.3:6: They married people from these nations and began serving their gods. It means small compromises in relationships and loyalty led Israel away from God.
entries.3:7: Israel did what was evil and forgot the Lord, serving false gods instead. It means forgetting God is not neutral; it quickly leads to serving other things.
entries.3:8: God's anger burned against Israel, and he let a Mesopotamian king rule over them for eight years. It means turning from God can bring real hardship and loss of freedom.
entries.3:9: When the people cried out to the Lord, he raised up Othniel to rescue them. It means God hears desperate prayers and provides help even after failure.
entries.3:10: God's Spirit empowered Othniel to lead and fight, and he defeated the Mesopotamian king. It means God gives strength and ability to the people he calls.
entries.3:11: The land had peace for forty years until Othniel died. It means faithful leadership brings real rest, but it can end when that leader is gone.
entries.3:12: Israel again did evil, so God made the Moabite king Eglon strong against them. It means repeated disobedience invites the same kind of trouble again.
entries.3:13: Eglon joined with Ammon and Amalek, defeated Israel, and captured the city of palms. It means enemies can team up when God's people are weak and divided.
entries.3:14: Israel served King Eglon for eighteen years. It means oppression can last a long time when people keep ignoring God.
entries.3:15: When Israel prayed, God gave them Ehud, a left-handed Benjamite, to rescue them. It means God often uses unlikely people and unexpected skills to save his people.
entries.3:16: Ehud made a short double-edged sword and hid it under his clothes on his right side. It means careful preparation can be part of how God delivers people.
entries.3:17: Ehud brought the tribute to Eglon, who was very fat. It means the story is setting the scene for what happens next.
entries.3:18: After delivering the offering, Ehud sent his companions away. It means he acted alone to carry out a dangerous plan.
entries.3:19: Ehud turned back and told the king he had a secret message, so the attendants were dismissed. It means secrecy and timing were part of his plan.
entries.3:20: Ehud told the king he had a message from God, and the king stood up from his seat. It means even a wicked king reacted when God's name was mentioned.
entries.3:21: Ehud drew the hidden sword with his left hand and thrust it into the king's belly. It means the rescue came through a sudden, violent act against the oppressor.
entries.3:22: The blade went in deep and the fat closed over it, and Ehud left without pulling it out. It means the king was struck down completely.
entries.3:23: Ehud went out through the covered way and locked the doors behind him. It means he escaped while the king's room was sealed off.
entries.3:24: The king's servants found the doors locked and assumed he was using the private room. It means their wrong assumption gave Ehud time to get away.
entries.3:25: They waited until embarrassed, then opened the doors and found their master dead on the floor. It means the truth finally became clear, but too late for them to stop Ehud.
entries.3:26: Ehud escaped while they waited, passed the stone images, and reached safety at Seirah. It means God's deliverer got away and lived to lead Israel.
entries.3:27: When Ehud arrived, he blew a horn in the hill country, and the Israelites gathered to follow him. It means a clear call can unite people for action.
entries.3:28: Ehud told Israel to follow him because God had given Moab into their hands, and they seized the Jordan crossings. It means God's promise gave them courage to act together.
entries.3:29: They killed about ten thousand strong Moabite fighting men, and none escaped. It means the victory was complete and decisive.
entries.3:30: Moab was defeated that day, and the land had peace for eighty years. It means God's rescue brought long-lasting rest to his people.
entries.3:31: After Ehud came Shamgar, who killed six hundred Philistines with an ox-goad and also saved Israel. It means God can use ordinary tools and ordinary people to deliver his people.
entries.4:1: Once their leader Ehud died, the Israelites went back to doing what God considered wrong. It shows how easily people drift back into bad habits when good leadership is gone.
entries.4:2: So God let a Canaanite king named Jabin, who ruled from Hazor, take control over them, with a commander named Sisera leading his army. The reader sees that turning from God can lead to being under hard rule.
entries.4:3: The Israelites cried out to God for help because Sisera had nine hundred iron chariots and had treated them cruelly for twenty years. It shows that God's people can call on him when life becomes unbearable.
entries.4:4: At that time a woman named Deborah, a prophet, was leading and judging Israel. It reminds us that God can raise up anyone, even those society might overlook, to lead.
entries.4:5: Deborah held court under a palm tree in the hill country, and people came to her to have their disputes settled. It pictures a leader who was accessible and trusted by the people.
entries.4:6: Deborah called Barak and told him God had commanded him to gather ten thousand men from two tribes and position them on Mount Tabor. It shows God giving clear direction through his chosen leader.
entries.4:7: God promised to draw Sisera and his chariots to the Kishon River and hand him over to Barak. The reader sees that God himself takes responsibility for the victory.
entries.4:8: Barak said he would only go if Deborah went with him. It shows a leader who wanted reassurance and support rather than acting alone.
entries.4:9: Deborah agreed to go but told Barak the credit would go to a woman instead of him, and then she went with him. It shows that hesitating to obey can cost us the honor we might have had.
entries.4:10: Barak gathered the ten thousand men at Kedesh, and Deborah went up with him. It shows the plan moving forward with both the military leader and the prophet together.
entries.4:11: A man named Heber, from a family related to Moses, had separated from his people and set up his tent near Kedesh. This detail sets up what happens later in the story.
entries.4:12: Sisera was told that Barak had gone up to Mount Tabor. It shows the enemy being alerted and preparing to respond.
entries.4:13: Sisera gathered all nine hundred of his iron chariots and his whole army and moved them to the Kishon River. It shows the overwhelming force lined up against Israel.
entries.4:14: Deborah urged Barak to attack right away because God had already given him the victory and was going ahead of him, so Barak led his men down the mountain. It shows that faith means acting when God says the time is now.
entries.4:15: God threw Sisera's whole army into panic before Barak, and Sisera jumped off his chariot and ran away on foot. It shows that God, not weapons, decides who wins.
entries.4:16: Barak chased the chariots and army all the way to Harosheth, and every enemy soldier was killed. It shows the victory was total, just as God had promised.
entries.4:17: Sisera ran on foot to the tent of Jael, whose husband's family was at peace with King Jabin. He thought he was running to a safe place.
entries.4:18: Jael came out and invited Sisera into her tent and told him not to be afraid, then covered him up. It shows him trusting someone who would turn out to be his undoing.
entries.4:19: Sisera asked for water, and Jael gave him milk to drink and covered him again. It shows her lulling him into a false sense of safety.
entries.4:20: Sisera told Jael to stand at the tent door and deny he was there if anyone asked. It shows him trying to hide and relying on her to protect him.
entries.4:21: While Sisera slept deeply from exhaustion, Jael quietly drove a tent peg through his head into the ground, killing him. It shows the victory coming through an unexpected person, exactly as Deborah had said.
entries.4:22: Jael met Barak chasing Sisera and showed him the dead man with the peg in his head. It confirms that God's word through Deborah came true.
entries.4:23: That day God defeated Jabin, the Canaanite king, in front of the Israelites. It shows God keeping his promise to rescue his people.
entries.4:24: Israel's strength kept growing against King Jabin until they finally destroyed him. It shows that God's deliverance, once started, was carried through to the end.
entries.5:1: Deborah and Barak sang this song together to celebrate a great victory. It shows that praising God for what he has done is a natural response to his help.
entries.5:2: The people volunteered willingly for battle, and the leaders led the way. God is worthy of praise when people freely give themselves to his cause.
entries.5:3: Deborah calls kings and rulers to listen because she is about to sing to the Lord, the God of Israel. The point is that God deserves attention and praise even from the powerful.
entries.5:4: This pictures God marching from the region of Edom with awesome power, shaking the earth and pouring rain from the clouds. It reminds the reader that God is a mighty warrior on behalf of his people.
entries.5:5: Even the mountains tremble when the Lord appears. Nothing in creation is stronger than God, so the reader can trust his power.
entries.5:6: In those days travel was so unsafe that people avoided the main roads and used hidden paths. It shows how much daily life suffers when there is no strong leadership or peace.
entries.5:7: Village life in Israel had collapsed until Deborah rose up to lead and care for the people like a mother. It shows how one faithful leader can restore a whole community.
entries.5:8: Israel had no weapons or shields because they were helpless against their enemies. It reminds the reader how vulnerable people are without God's help.
entries.5:9: Deborah calls the leaders and the willing volunteers to join her in praising the Lord. Those who step forward to serve should give God the credit.
entries.5:10: Those who ride fine donkeys and those who walk the roads should think about what God has done. Everyone, rich or poor, should stop and consider God's acts.
entries.5:11: At the watering places people retell the story of God's righteous deeds for Israel. It is good to remember and repeat what God has done so others hear it too.
entries.5:12: Deborah stirs herself and Barak to rise up and sing, and Barak is called to lead his captives away. God's victory should wake us up to action and praise.
entries.5:13: The leaders and the people of God came down together to join the fight. God's work gets done when leaders and ordinary people move together.
entries.5:14: Warriors from several tribes came down to join the battle. Different groups united for a common cause, showing the value of standing together.
entries.5:15: Issachar's leaders stood with Deborah and Naphtali with Barak, but Reuben was divided and unsure. It warns the reader that hesitation and inner conflict keep people from joining God's work.
entries.5:16: Reuben stayed home among the sheep instead of joining the fight. It points out the shame of sitting safely by while others risk everything.
entries.5:17: Gilead, Dan, and Asher stayed in their own comfortable places instead of helping. It shows how easy it is to make excuses and avoid responsibility.
entries.5:18: Zebulun and Naphtali risked their lives on the battlefield. Their courage is held up as an example of real commitment.
entries.5:19: The Canaanite kings fought hard at Megiddo but gained nothing. It shows that opposing God's people brings no lasting profit.
entries.5:20: Even the stars are pictured as fighting against Sisera from the sky. The whole creation is on God's side, so no enemy can ultimately win.
entries.5:21: The Kishon River swept the enemy away in flood. Deborah praises God for using nature itself to rescue his people.
entries.5:22: The sound of galloping horses shows the enemy fleeing in panic. It is a vivid picture of how quickly God can turn a battle around.
entries.5:23: An angel curses the town of Meroz for refusing to help the Lord's cause. It warns the reader that standing aside when help is needed is a serious failure.
entries.5:24: Jael is praised above all women for what she did. Her courage shows that God can use unexpected people to accomplish great things.
entries.5:25: Sisera asked for water and Jael gave him milk and rich food, treating him like an honored guest. It sets up the surprise of what happens next.
entries.5:26: Jael took a tent peg and a hammer and struck Sisera's head. A woman with simple tools defeated a powerful enemy, showing God's strength in unlikely hands.
entries.5:27: Sisera fell dead at Jael's feet. The mighty commander ended in total defeat, proving that human power cannot stand against God's purposes.
entries.5:28: Sisera's mother waited at the window, wondering why her son's chariot was so late. It shows the sad human cost of war, even for the enemy's family.
entries.5:29: Her wise women tried to reassure her with guesses about the delay. Their false comfort shows how people convince themselves that all is well when it is not.
entries.5:30: They imagined the soldiers dividing up plunder, including women and fine colored cloth. Their hopeful guesses were tragically wrong, showing how empty human confidence can be.
entries.5:31: The song ends by asking God to destroy all his enemies while those who love him shine like the sun, and the land had peace for forty years. It reminds the reader that God's victory brings lasting peace for those who trust him.
entries.6:1: Israel did what God considered wrong, so God let the Midianites defeat and rule over them for seven years. Doing wrong can bring real trouble into our lives.
entries.6:2: The Midianites were too strong for Israel, so the people hid in caves and secret holes in the rocks. Fear can make people run and hide instead of living freely.
entries.6:3: Every time Israel planted crops, the Midianites and their allies attacked them. Enemies can keep showing up and destroying what you have worked for.
entries.6:4: The raiders camped on the land and took every crop as far as Gaza, leaving no food and no animals in Israel. Everything the people depended on was stripped away.
entries.6:5: The invaders came with their animals and tents in huge numbers like a swarm of locusts, and their camels could not be counted. They came only to destroy the land.
entries.6:6: Israel was brought very low by Midian, and the people finally cried out to the Lord for help. Hitting bottom can turn people back to God.
entries.6:7: When the Israelites cried out to the Lord because of Midian's oppression, God heard them. God listens when people call to him in their distress.
entries.6:8: God sent a prophet to remind Israel that he was the one who brought them out of slavery in Egypt. God reminds us of what he has already done for us.
entries.6:9: God reminded them that he rescued them from the Egyptians and from all who treated them cruelly, driving those enemies out and giving Israel their land. God's past rescue is a reason to trust him now.
entries.6:10: God had told them not to worship the gods of the Amorites whose land they lived in, but they refused to listen. Ignoring God's clear instruction is what got them into trouble.
entries.6:11: The angel of the Lord came and sat under an oak tree in Ophrah, where Gideon was secretly threshing grain in a winepress to hide it from the Midianites. God shows up in ordinary, hidden places.
entries.6:12: The angel of the Lord appeared to Gideon and greeted him as a mighty warrior, saying the Lord was with him. God can see strength in someone who feels weak and afraid.
entries.6:13: Gideon questioned the greeting, asking why all this trouble had come if God was with them, and where God's mighty deeds were that their ancestors had told about. It is honest to bring our doubts and hard questions to God.
entries.6:14: The Lord turned to Gideon and told him to go with the strength he had and save Israel from Midian, because God was sending him. God calls ordinary people to do his work.
entries.6:15: Gideon objected that his family was the weakest in Manasseh and he was the least important in his father's house. Feeling small does not disqualify you from God's call.
entries.6:16: The Lord promised to be with Gideon, and said he would defeat the Midianites as easily as if they were one man. God's presence is what makes an impossible task possible.
entries.6:17: Gideon asked for a sign to confirm that it was really God speaking to him. God is patient with people who honestly want to be sure.
entries.6:18: Gideon asked the angel to wait while he brought an offering, and the angel agreed to stay until he returned. God can wait while we bring him our worship.
entries.6:19: Gideon prepared a young goat, bread made without yeast, and broth, and brought it out to the angel under the oak tree. Giving our best to God is a fitting response to his call.
entries.6:20: The angel of God told Gideon to place the meat and bread on the rock and pour out the broth, and Gideon did as he was told. Obeying God's instructions, even odd ones, matters.
entries.6:21: The angel touched the food with his staff, fire came out of the rock and burned it up, and then the angel disappeared. This confirmed that Gideon's visitor was truly from God.
entries.6:22: Gideon realized he had seen the angel of the Lord face to face and was terrified he would die. Encountering God's presence can fill us with awe and fear.
entries.6:23: The Lord told Gideon to have peace and not be afraid, because he would not die. God calms our fear when we come close to him.
entries.6:24: Gideon built an altar there and named it 'The Lord is peace,' and it remained in Ophrah. Remembering God's peace helps us hold onto it.
entries.6:25: That night the Lord told Gideon to take ten servants and a seven-year-old ox, tear down his father's altar to Baal, and cut down the sacred pole beside it. God sometimes asks us to deal with wrong things close to home.
entries.6:26: God told Gideon to build a proper altar to the Lord on top of the rock and to sacrifice the ox using the wood of the cut-down pole. God replaces false worship with true worship.
entries.6:27: Gideon took ten servants and did what God said, but he did it at night because he was afraid of his family and the townspeople. Fear can make us obey God quietly, but God still uses that obedience.
entries.6:28: In the morning the townspeople found Baal's altar broken down, the sacred pole cut, and the ox sacrificed on the new altar. Wrong done in secret still becomes visible.
entries.6:29: The people asked each other who had done this, and after careful searching they concluded it was Gideon, son of Joash. Our actions, even hidden ones, eventually point back to us.
entries.6:30: The townsmen demanded that Joash bring out his son Gideon to be put to death for tearing down Baal's altar and cutting the sacred pole. Standing against popular idols can bring serious opposition.
entries.6:31: Joash told the angry crowd that if Baal is a god, he can defend himself, and anyone who takes up Baal's cause should be put to death by morning. A false god cannot defend itself, so its followers must fight for it.
entries.6:32: That day Joash gave Gideon the name Jerubbaal, meaning 'let Baal contend with him,' because Gideon had broken down Baal's altar. The name became a public challenge to the false god.
entries.6:33: The Midianites, Amalekites, and eastern peoples joined forces, crossed over, and camped in the Jezreel Valley. The threat against Israel was gathering and growing.
entries.6:34: The Spirit of the Lord came upon Gideon, and when he blew the trumpet, his clan gathered behind him. God's Spirit empowers ordinary people to lead.
entries.6:35: Gideon sent messengers throughout Manasseh, Asher, Zebulun, and Naphtali, and men from those tribes came up to join him. God's call can draw many people together for a common purpose.
entries.6:36: Gideon asked God to confirm that he would really save Israel through him, as God had promised. Even after God's call, Gideon wanted assurance.
entries.6:37: Gideon proposed a test: if the fleece had dew on it while the ground stayed dry, he would know God would save Israel through him. Asking God for confirmation shows both faith and doubt.
entries.6:38: It happened just as Gideon asked: the next morning he wrung out the fleece and got a bowl full of water. God graciously answered Gideon's request.
entries.6:39: Gideon asked God not to be angry if he made one more test, this time asking for the fleece to be dry while dew covered the ground. God's patience with our weakness is remarkable.
entries.6:40: That night God did exactly that: the fleece was dry and the ground around it was wet with dew. God confirmed his promise a second time, showing patience with Gideon's need for certainty.
entries.7:1: Gideon and his army camped by a spring while the Midianite army camped nearby in the valley. The two sides were close enough to fight, setting the scene for what God was about to do.
entries.7:2: God told Gideon his army was too big, because the people would brag that they saved themselves instead of giving God the credit. It reminds us that God wants us to trust him rather than our own strength.
entries.7:3: God told Gideon to send home anyone who was afraid, and twenty-two thousand left, leaving only ten thousand. God does not want people fighting for him out of fear or pressure.
entries.7:4: God said there were still too many men and told Gideon to bring them to the water so he could show which ones to keep. God was choosing the army himself, not leaving it to human judgment.
entries.7:5: At the water, God told Gideon to separate the men into two groups based on how they drank. This unusual test was God's way of narrowing down the army.
entries.7:6: Only three hundred men drank by lapping water with their tongues, while everyone else knelt down to drink. The small group would become God's chosen force.
entries.7:7: God promised to save Israel through just those three hundred men and told Gideon to send everyone else home. God often works through small numbers so the victory clearly comes from him.
entries.7:8: Gideon kept the three hundred and sent the rest home, taking their supplies and horns for the men who stayed. The Midianite army was still camped below them in the valley.
entries.7:9: That night God told Gideon to go down and attack, promising he had already given the enemy into his hands. God gave clear direction and assurance before the battle.
entries.7:10: God offered Gideon a way to deal with his fear by taking his servant Purah with him. God is patient with our fears and gives us help to face them.
entries.7:11: God said that hearing what the enemy was saying would give Gideon courage to attack, so he went down to the edge of the enemy camp. Encouragement can come from unexpected places when we need it.
entries.7:12: The enemy army was huge, filling the valley like locusts, with camels too many to count. The odds looked impossible, which makes what happens next clearly God's doing.
entries.7:13: Gideon overheard a man telling a dream about a barley loaf rolling into the Midianite camp and flattening a tent. The dream was a sign that pointed to Israel's victory.
entries.7:14: The man's friend interpreted the dream as meaning God had given the whole Midianite army into Gideon's hands. The enemy themselves were saying God was on Israel's side.
entries.7:15: When Gideon heard the dream and its meaning, he worshiped God, then went back and told his men to get up because God had given them the victory. Worship and courage came together after he received this sign.
entries.7:16: Gideon divided the three hundred men into three groups and gave each man a horn and a jar with a burning torch inside. The plan relied on surprise and noise rather than weapons.
entries.7:17: Gideon told his men to watch him and copy exactly what he did when they reached the enemy camp. He led by example and asked them to follow his lead.
entries.7:18: When Gideon and his group blew their horns, everyone was to blow theirs too and shout that the battle belonged to the Lord and to Gideon. The shout declared who was really fighting for them.
entries.7:19: Gideon and his men reached the edge of the camp at the start of the middle watch, just as guards had taken their posts, and they blew horns and smashed their jars. The timing caught the enemy off guard.
entries.7:20: All three groups blew their horns, broke their jars, held up their torches, and shouted that the battle was for the Lord and for Gideon. The noise and light made a small force seem much larger.
entries.7:21: The men stood in place around the camp while the enemy woke up in confusion and ran away shouting. God caused panic without Israel needing to swing a sword.
entries.7:22: As the three hundred blew their horns, God turned the enemy's swords against each other, and the army fled far away. The victory came from God, not from Israel's fighting.
entries.7:23: Men from Naphtali, Asher, and Manasseh joined together and chased the fleeing Midianites. The people who had gone home earlier were now called back to help finish the job.
entries.7:24: Gideon sent word through Ephraim to block the escape routes at the Jordan River, and the men of Ephraim gathered to do it. The enemy was being cut off from getting away.
entries.7:25: The Ephraimites captured and killed two Midianite leaders, Oreb and Zeeb, and brought their heads to Gideon across the Jordan. The victory was completed, and the enemy's leaders were defeated.
entries.8:1: The tribe of Ephraim was angry because Gideon had not invited them to the main battle, and they complained loudly. It shows how quickly people can feel slighted even when a great victory has just been won.
entries.8:2: Gideon answered gently, saying their small share in the victory was worth more than everything his own group had done. A soft, humble reply can calm an angry person.
entries.8:3: Gideon pointed out that God had let Ephraim capture the enemy leaders, which was a greater honor than his own part. His humble words turned their anger into goodwill toward him.
entries.8:4: Gideon and his three hundred men crossed the Jordan River, exhausted and hungry from the chase. Even people doing God's work can reach the end of their strength and need help.
entries.8:5: Gideon asked the town of Succoth for bread for his tired soldiers while he kept chasing the two enemy kings. It was a simple, reasonable request for help from fellow Israelites.
entries.8:6: The leaders of Succoth refused, mocking Gideon by asking whether he had already captured the enemy kings. They were betting against him and would not risk helping.
entries.8:7: Gideon warned that once the Lord gave him victory, he would punish Succoth's leaders severely for their refusal. He was promising harsh justice, not making an idle threat.
entries.8:8: Gideon asked the people of Penuel for help too, and they gave the same refusal as Succoth. The same lack of support was spreading to another town.
entries.8:9: Gideon told Penuel that when he returned safely, he would tear down their tower. He was warning them that their refusal would not be forgotten.
entries.8:10: The enemy kings were camped at Karkor with about fifteen thousand men left, since a hundred and twenty thousand had already been killed. The enemy was weakened but still a real threat.
entries.8:11: Gideon took a hidden desert route and attacked the enemy camp while they felt safe and unsuspecting. A surprise attack caught them off guard.
entries.8:12: The two kings fled, but Gideon chased them down and captured them, and his men defeated the rest of the army. The victory was complete.
entries.8:13: Gideon returned from the battle. The story now turns to how he dealt with the towns that had refused to help him.
entries.8:14: Gideon caught a young man from Succoth and got him to write down the names of the town's leaders, seventy-seven in all. He was gathering evidence before confronting them.
entries.8:15: Gideon showed the captured kings to the men of Succoth and reminded them of their mocking words. He proved them wrong about his success.
entries.8:16: Gideon carried out his earlier threat, punishing the leaders of Succoth with thorns and sharp branches. He kept the harsh promise he had made.
entries.8:17: Gideon also tore down the tower of Penuel and killed the men of that town. Both towns paid a heavy price for refusing to help.
entries.8:18: Gideon asked the captured kings about the men they had killed at Tabor, and they admitted those men had looked like princes. Gideon was about to learn they were his own relatives.
entries.8:19: Gideon revealed that the men killed were his own brothers, and he swore that if the kings had spared them, he would have let the kings live. This was personal grief, not just war.
entries.8:20: Gideon told his oldest son to kill the kings, but the boy was afraid and did not draw his sword because he was still young. Killing in battle was too much for a boy.
entries.8:21: The kings told Gideon to finish them himself, since he was a man, so Gideon killed them and took the ornaments from their camels. The enemy leaders met their end at his own hand.
entries.8:22: The Israelites asked Gideon to rule over them and his descendants after him, because he had saved them from Midian. They wanted a king-like ruler to reward their hero.
entries.8:23: Gideon refused to be their ruler and said his son would not rule either, because the Lord was their true ruler. He pointed them back to God rather than to himself.
entries.8:24: Gideon asked the people to give him the gold earrings they had taken from the enemy. It seemed like a modest request after such a victory.
entries.8:25: The people gladly agreed and spread out a cloak for everyone to drop their earrings into. They were eager to honor Gideon.
entries.8:26: The gold earrings weighed about seventeen hundred shekels, not counting the kings' ornaments, robes, and camel chains. It was a large amount of treasure.
entries.8:27: Gideon made a special priestly garment, an ephod, from the gold and set it up in his town, and all Israel worshiped it there instead of God. What began as a memorial became a snare that led Gideon's family and the nation into sin.
entries.8:28: Midian was defeated and never regained its power, and the land had peace for forty years during Gideon's lifetime. God gave Israel lasting rest after the victory.
entries.8:29: Gideon, also called Jerubbaal, went home and lived there. After the fighting, he returned to ordinary life.
entries.8:30: Gideon had seventy sons because he had many wives. His large family would later become a source of trouble.
entries.8:31: A servant-wife in Shechem bore him a son named Abimelech. This son would later cause great harm to Gideon's family.
entries.8:32: Gideon died at a good old age and was buried in his father's tomb in Ophrah. His long life ended peacefully.
entries.8:33: After Gideon died, the Israelites turned back to worshiping the gods of Canaan and made Baal-berith their god. They quickly forgot the Lord who had saved them.
entries.8:34: The people did not remember the Lord their God, who had rescued them from all their enemies. Forgetting God's past help led them straight back into false worship.
entries.8:35: They also failed to show kindness to Gideon's family, despite all the good he had done for Israel. People easily forget the ones who helped them.
entries.9:1: Abimelech went to his mother's relatives in Shechem to get their support. He was building a power base among people who were tied to him by family.
entries.9:2: He asked them to compare being ruled by seventy men versus just one man, and reminded them he was their own relative. He was using family loyalty to win their backing for himself.
entries.9:3: His relatives repeated his case to the town leaders, and the people sided with Abimelech because he was one of their own. They chose him based on family ties rather than what was right.
entries.9:4: They paid him money from a temple treasury, and he used it to hire reckless troublemakers as his followers. He was building a gang of thugs to seize power.
entries.9:5: He went to his father's house and killed all seventy of his brothers on one stone, but the youngest, Jotham, hid and survived. Abimelech murdered his own family to remove anyone who could challenge him.
entries.9:6: The people of Shechem and Beth-millo gathered and made Abimelech king. The town that had helped him now crowned him.
entries.9:7: When Jotham heard what happened, he stood on a mountain and shouted to the people of Shechem to listen to him, so that God would listen to them. The lone survivor was about to confront the town that backed his brother's crime.
entries.9:8: Jotham told a story about trees that decided they wanted a king. He used this made-up tale to make a point about the people's choice.
entries.9:9: In the story, the olive tree refused to be king because it did not want to give up the valuable oil that honors God and people. It shows that a good, useful person does not chase power at the cost of their real purpose.
entries.9:10: The trees then asked the fig tree to be their king. They kept looking for someone willing to take the job.
entries.9:11: The fig tree also refused, saying it would not give up its sweet fruit just to wave over the other trees. Like the olive, it valued its useful work more than empty status.
entries.9:12: Next the trees asked the vine to rule over them. The story keeps showing that the worthwhile plants turn the offer down.
entries.9:13: The vine refused too, because it did not want to give up the wine that brings joy to God and people. The point is that the best candidates never wanted the crown.
entries.9:14: Finally the trees went to the thorn bush and asked it to be their king. Only the useless, dangerous plant was willing.
entries.9:15: The thorn bush agreed only if they truly trusted it, and warned that if not, fire would come from it and burn even the great cedars. The one who takes power is dangerous and will turn on those who chose him.
entries.9:16: Jotham told the people to judge for themselves whether they had acted honestly and fairly toward his father's family by making Abimelech king. He was putting their actions on trial.
entries.9:17: He reminded them that his father had fought for them and risked his life to free them from Midian. They owed a debt to the man whose sons they had just killed.
entries.9:18: He pointed out that they had turned on his father's family, killed seventy of his sons, and made the son of a servant woman king just because he was their relative. Their choice was based on favoritism, not justice.
entries.9:19: He said that if they had acted honestly toward his father's family, then they and Abimelech could enjoy each other. He was giving them a chance to admit they had done right.
entries.9:20: But if they had not acted honestly, he called down a curse that fire would come from Abimelech against them and from them against Abimelech. He was predicting that their partnership would destroy both sides.
entries.9:21: Then Jotham fled to Beer and lived there out of fear of his brother Abimelech. The last surviving brother had to run for his life.
entries.9:22: Abimelech ruled over Israel for three years. His reign was short.
entries.9:23: God sent a spirit of distrust between Abimelech and the people of Shechem, and they turned against him. The alliance that was built on murder began to fall apart.
entries.9:24: This happened so that the guilt for killing the seventy sons would fall on Abimelech and on the people of Shechem who helped him. God was making sure the crime did not go unpunished.
entries.9:25: The people of Shechem set ambushes on the mountain roads and robbed everyone passing by, and Abimelech heard about it. The town that made him king was now working against him.
entries.9:26: A man named Gaal came with his brothers and won the trust of the people of Shechem. A new rival appeared on the scene.
entries.9:27: They harvested their grapes, held a feast in their god's temple, and cursed Abimelech while they ate and drank. Their loyalty to him had turned into open contempt.
entries.9:28: Gaal asked who Abimelech really was that they should serve him, and argued they should be free of him and his officer Zebul. He stirred up the town against its king.
entries.9:29: Gaal wished he had authority over the people so he could get rid of Abimelech and challenge him to bring his army out. He was boasting about what he would do if he were in charge.
entries.9:30: Zebul, the town's ruler, heard what Gaal said and became angry. He was loyal to Abimelech and did not accept the challenge.
entries.9:31: Zebul secretly sent word to Abimelech that Gaal and his brothers had come and were turning the town against him. He warned the king about the plot.
entries.9:32: He told Abimelech to move at night with his men and hide in the fields. He gave him a plan for a surprise attack.
entries.9:33: In the morning, when the sun came up, he should rush the town and deal with Gaal and his men however he could. The plan was to strike early and catch them off guard.
entries.9:34: So Abimelech and his men got up at night and split into four groups to ambush Shechem. They set the trap.
entries.9:35: Gaal went out and stood at the town gate, and then Abimelech and his men rose from their hiding place. The ambush was sprung.
entries.9:36: When Gaal saw the men, he told Zebul that people were coming down from the mountains, but Zebul pretended it was just the shadows of the hills. He was stalling and covering for Abimelech.
entries.9:37: Gaal insisted again that he saw men coming down from the middle of the land and one group by the oak of the Seers. He was not fooled by Zebul's excuse.
entries.9:38: Zebul mocked him, asking where his big talk was now, and told him to go out and fight the very people he had insulted. He threw Gaal's earlier boasting back in his face.
entries.9:39: So Gaal led the men of Shechem out and fought against Abimelech. He had to back up his words with action.
entries.9:40: Abimelech chased him, and Gaal ran away, and many men fell dead by the sword all the way back to the town gate. Gaal's rebellion was crushed quickly.
entries.9:41: Abimelech stayed in Arumah while Zebul forced Gaal and his relatives out of Shechem, refusing to let them live there. This shows that the challenge to Abimelech's power was crushed and his rivals were expelled from the city.
entries.9:42: The next day the people of Shechem went out into the fields, and Abimelech was told about it. Their ordinary activity gave Abimelech the chance he was waiting for.
entries.9:43: Abimelech split his men into three groups and hid them in the fields, then attacked when he saw the people leaving the town. He used a planned ambush rather than an open fight, catching the townspeople off guard.
entries.9:44: Abimelech's group rushed to block the town gate while the other two groups attacked everyone out in the fields and defeated them. The town was trapped and its people outside were cut off.
entries.9:45: Abimelech fought the town all day, captured it, killed its people, and destroyed it, scattering salt over it. Spreading salt was a sign that the place was meant to stay ruined and unusable.
entries.9:46: When the people at the tower of Shechem heard what happened to the town, they crowded into the inner room of the temple of El-berith. They ran to a place they thought was safe, a strong building tied to their worship.
entries.9:47: Abimelech was told that all the men of the tower of Shechem had gathered in one place. Their hiding place became known to him, setting up what he did next.
entries.9:48: Abimelech went up Mount Zalmon, cut branches with an axe, carried them on his back, and told his men to copy him quickly. He was preparing a mass attack using wood as fuel.
entries.9:49: Every man cut a branch, and they piled the wood against the inner room and set it on fire, burning about a thousand men and women inside. The people who sought safety in the temple died there.
entries.9:50: Abimelech then went to Thebez, set up his army against it, and captured it. His campaign of conquest continued to the next town.
entries.9:51: In the middle of Thebez was a strong tower, and all the men and women fled into it, locked themselves in, and went up on its roof. They hoped the tower would protect them from the attack.
entries.9:52: Abimelech came to the tower and attacked it, getting close to its door so he could set it on fire. He was about to repeat the burning tactic that had worked before.
entries.9:53: A woman dropped a heavy upper millstone on Abimelech's head and cracked his skull. The mighty attacker was brought down by an unexpected person in a single blow.
entries.9:54: Abimelech quickly told his servant to run him through with a sword so people would not say a woman killed him, and the servant did so. His concern for his reputation mattered to him even as he was dying.
entries.9:55: When the men of Israel saw that Abimelech was dead, they all went home. His death ended the campaign and scattered his army.
entries.9:56: In this way God repaid Abimelech for the evil he did to his father by killing his seventy brothers. The story presents his downfall as God's justice for his crimes.
entries.9:57: God also brought back on the men of Shechem the evil they had done, and Jotham's curse came true on them. The passage says both the cruel ruler and the treacherous city got what their actions deserved.
entries.10:1: After Abimelech died, a man named Tola from the tribe of Issachar stepped up and rescued Israel from trouble. He lived in Shamir, in the hill country of Ephraim, and God used him to bring help to his people.
entries.10:2: Tola led Israel as judge for twenty-three years, and when he died he was buried in Shamir. His long, steady leadership was a quiet gift to the nation.
entries.10:3: After Tola, a man named Jair from Gilead led Israel for twenty-two years. Like Tola, he gave the people a long stretch of stable leadership.
entries.10:4: Jair had thirty sons, and each one rode his own donkey and was in charge of a town in Gilead; those towns were still called Havvoth-Jair when this was written. This showed how much honor and influence Jair's family had.
entries.10:5: When Jair died, he was buried in Kamon. His story ends simply, with his body laid to rest like the judges before him.
entries.10:6: Once again the Israelites did what was evil in God's eyes, worshiping the false gods of many surrounding nations instead of the Lord. They abandoned the God who had rescued them and served idols instead.
entries.10:7: God's anger burned against Israel, and he let the Philistines and the Ammonites gain power over them. Turning away from God brought real, painful consequences.
entries.10:8: That same year those enemies crushed and oppressed the Israelites, especially those east of the Jordan in Gilead, for eighteen long years. The suffering was severe and lasted a long time.
entries.10:9: The Ammonites crossed the Jordan to attack Judah, Benjamin, and Ephraim, so Israel was in deep distress. The trouble reached the heart of the nation.
entries.10:10: The Israelites cried out to the Lord and admitted they had sinned by abandoning him and serving the Baals. Honest confession was their first step back toward God.
entries.10:11: The Lord reminded Israel of all the times he had rescued them from the Egyptians, the Amorites, the Ammonites, and the Philistines. He wanted them to remember his faithful help in the past.
entries.10:12: God also recalled saving them from the Sidonians, Amalekites, and Midianites whenever they cried out to him. His record of rescue was long and clear.
entries.10:13: But God said that despite all this, they had abandoned him and served other gods, so he would no longer rescue them. Their repeated betrayal had worn out his patience.
entries.10:14: God told them to go cry out to the gods they had chosen and let those gods save them in their trouble. He was showing them how useless their idols really were.
entries.10:15: The Israelites admitted their sin and asked God to do whatever he thought right, begging only for rescue that day. They stopped making excuses and threw themselves on God's mercy.
entries.10:16: So they got rid of the foreign gods among them and served the Lord again, and God could no longer bear to see Israel's suffering. Their repentance moved him to compassion.
entries.10:17: The Ammonites gathered and set up camp in Gilead, and the Israelites assembled and camped at Mizpah. The two armies were now facing each other for battle.
entries.10:18: The Israelites asked each other who would lead the attack against the Ammonites, and they promised to make that person the leader over all Gilead. They were looking for someone brave enough to take charge.
entries.11:1: Jephthah was a skilled fighter, but his mother was not married to his father, which made people look down on him. Your worth is not decided by your family background.
entries.11:2: When his half-brothers grew up, they forced Jephthah out and refused to let him share the family inheritance because of who his mother was. Being rejected by family hurts, but it does not mean God is finished with you.
entries.11:3: Jephthah ran away from his brothers and settled in another region, where a group of rough men gathered around him and went out raiding with him. Trouble and rejection can push people toward hard company.
entries.11:4: Some time later, the Ammonites went to war against Israel. Trouble often comes when you least expect it.
entries.11:5: When the Ammonites attacked, the leaders of Gilead went to bring Jephthah back from the land of Tob. People often remember those they pushed away only when they need them.
entries.11:6: The leaders asked Jephthah to come and lead them in the fight against the Ammonites. They were offering him the very role his family had denied him.
entries.11:7: Jephthah reminded them that they had hated him and thrown him out, and asked why they were coming to him now that they were in trouble. It is fair to name past wrongs honestly.
entries.11:8: The leaders admitted they needed him and promised to make him ruler over all Gilead if he would lead them. A real apology includes making things right.
entries.11:9: Jephthah asked them to confirm that if the Lord gave him victory, they would truly make him their leader. It is wise to settle clear terms before agreeing to something big.
entries.11:10: The leaders swore before the Lord that they would do exactly as they promised. A promise made before God is meant to be kept.
entries.11:11: So Jephthah went with the leaders, and the people made him their head and chief, and he repeated his words before the Lord at Mizpah. God can lift someone from rejection to leadership.
entries.11:12: Jephthah sent messengers to the Ammonite king asking why he had come to attack his land. It is better to ask questions and talk before fighting.
entries.11:13: The Ammonite king claimed that Israel had taken his land when they came out of Egypt and demanded it back peacefully. Not every claim people make is actually true.
entries.11:14: Jephthah sent messengers back to the Ammonite king again. He was willing to keep the conversation going rather than rush into war.
entries.11:15: Jephthah's reply was that Israel had not taken the land of Moab or the land of the Ammonites. He answered the accusation with facts.
entries.11:16: He explained that when Israel came up from Egypt, they traveled through the desert to the Red Sea and arrived at Kadesh. He was laying out the history step by step.
entries.11:17: Israel asked Edom and then Moab for permission to pass through their land, but both refused, so Israel stayed at Kadesh. Israel did not simply take what it wanted.
entries.11:18: Israel then went around Edom and Moab through the desert and camped on the far side of the Arnon River without entering Moab's territory. They respected the borders of other nations.
entries.11:19: Israel then asked Sihon, king of the Amorites, for permission to pass through his land on the way to their own place. They kept trying the peaceful route.
entries.11:20: Sihon refused and gathered his army at Jahaz to attack Israel. Sometimes others choose the fight even when you seek peace.
entries.11:21: The Lord gave Sihon and his people into Israel's hands, and Israel took possession of the Amorites' land. The victory was credited to God, not to Israel's own strength.
entries.11:22: Israel gained the whole territory of the Amorites, from the Arnon to the Jabbok and from the desert to the Jordan. The land in dispute had come from the Amorites, not the Ammonites.
entries.11:23: Jephthah argued that since the Lord had taken the land from the Amorites and given it to Israel, the Ammonites had no right to it. What God gives, people should not try to grab back.
entries.11:24: Jephthah pointed out that the Ammonites kept whatever land their god Chemosh gave them, so Israel would keep what the Lord their God gave them. People usually defend what they believe their god gives them.
entries.11:25: Jephthah asked whether the Ammonites were any better than Balak, the Moabite king, who never fought Israel over this land. Pride often makes people claim more than their history supports.
entries.11:26: He noted that Israel had lived in these towns for three hundred years, and the Ammonites never tried to take them back during all that time. A claim made only after centuries is hard to believe.
entries.11:27: Jephthah insisted he had done nothing wrong and that the Ammonites were the ones doing wrong, and he asked the Lord, the judge, to decide between them. When you are in the right, you can leave the verdict with God.
entries.11:28: The Ammonite king ignored everything Jephthah said. Some people will not listen to reason, no matter how clearly you explain.
entries.11:29: The Spirit of the Lord came on Jephthah, and he passed through Gilead and Manasseh and on to Mizpah of Gilead, then crossed over toward the Ammonites. God's Spirit can empower ordinary people for hard tasks.
entries.11:30: Jephthah made a vow to the Lord, promising something if God gave him victory. Making rash promises to God can lead to deep trouble.
entries.11:31: He promised that whoever first came out of his house to meet him after the victory would belong to the Lord and be offered as a burned offering. This was a reckless vow, and it would cost him dearly.
entries.11:32: Jephthah crossed over to fight the Ammonites, and the Lord gave them into his hands. God answered his prayer for victory.
entries.11:33: He struck them down from Aroer all the way to Minnith, capturing twenty towns and reaching Abel-cheramim, and the Ammonites were defeated before Israel. The victory was complete and decisive.
entries.11:34: When Jephthah came home to Mizpah, his daughter came out to meet him with music and dancing, and she was his only child. The very person he feared most in his vow was the one who came out.
entries.11:35: When he saw her, he was shattered with grief and told her she was the cause of his trouble, because he had made a vow to the Lord and could not take it back. A hasty promise can bring pain to the people we love most.
entries.11:36: She told him to do as he had vowed, since the Lord had given him victory over his enemies. She showed remarkable trust and courage in a terrible situation.
entries.11:37: She asked only for two months to go into the mountains with her friends and mourn her fate. Even in sorrow, she asked for time to grieve.
entries.11:38: He sent her away for two months, and she went with her friends into the mountains and wept over what was to come. Grief needs time and space.
entries.11:39: After two months she returned, and he did to her as he had vowed, and she had never been with a man; and this became a custom in Israel. This is a tragic story of a vow kept at a terrible cost.
entries.11:40: Each year the women of Israel went out for four days to mourn the daughter of Jephthah the Gileadite. People remembered her sorrow year after year, and her story was not forgotten.
entries.12:1: The tribe of Ephraim was angry that Jephthah fought Ammon without inviting them, and they threatened to burn down his house. It shows how pride and hurt feelings can turn allies into enemies.
entries.12:2: Jephthah answers that his people were in real danger and he did call for help, but Ephraim never came. He is pointing out that their anger is unfair because they ignored him when he needed them.
entries.12:3: Jephthah says he risked his life because no help came, and God gave him the victory. He asks why they now want to fight him instead of celebrating what God did.
entries.12:4: Jephthah gathered the men of Gilead and fought Ephraim, and Gilead won. A dispute between fellow Israelites turned into a bloody civil war.
entries.12:5: The Gileadites seized the Jordan River crossings so fleeing Ephraimites could not escape, and they questioned anyone trying to cross about which tribe they belonged to. It shows how the conflict cut off any safe way out.
entries.12:6: They used a word test: Ephraimites could not pronounce "Shibboleth" correctly, and those who failed were killed at the river. The passage reports that forty-two thousand died, a tragic result of pride and revenge.
entries.12:7: Jephthah led Israel for six years and then died, and he was buried in his own town in Gilead. His story ends with a short, quiet note after all the fighting.
entries.12:8: After Jephthah, Ibzan from Bethlehem became the leader of Israel. The account moves on to a new judge.
entries.12:9: Ibzan had thirty sons and thirty daughters, and he arranged marriages for all of them outside his clan. He led Israel for seven years, which shows his wealth and status.
entries.12:10: Ibzan died and was buried in Bethlehem. His time as leader is summed up briefly.
entries.12:11: After Ibzan, Elon from the tribe of Zebulun led Israel for ten years. The story simply records his term.
entries.12:12: Elon died and was buried in Aijalon, in the land of Zebulun. Like the other judges, his life ends with a burial notice.
entries.12:13: After Elon, Abdon son of Hillel from Pirathon became the leader of Israel. The account introduces another judge.
entries.12:14: Abdon had forty sons and thirty grandsons who rode seventy donkeys, a sign of wealth and importance. He led Israel for eight years.
entries.12:15: Abdon died and was buried in Pirathon, in the hill country of Ephraim. His brief record closes this section of judges.
entries.13:1: Israel did wrong again in God's eyes, so he let the Philistines rule over them for forty years. It shows that turning away from God brings hard consequences, even for a long time.
entries.13:2: A man named Manoah from the tribe of Dan lived in Zorah, and his wife had never been able to have children. Their childlessness sets up the story of a surprising gift from God.
entries.13:3: The angel of the Lord told the woman she would finally become pregnant and have a son. God was answering a long, painful wait with a promise.
entries.13:4: The angel told her to avoid wine, strong drink, and anything ritually unclean while pregnant. Her son was being set apart for God from before he was born.
entries.13:5: Her son must never cut his hair because he was dedicated to God from birth, and he would begin to rescue Israel from the Philistines. God was raising up a deliverer for his people.
entries.13:6: The woman told her husband about the visitor, describing him as awe-inspiring like an angel and saying she hadn't asked where he came from. She shared the startling news honestly with her husband.
entries.13:7: She repeated the angel's words: she would have a son, she must avoid wine and unclean food, and the boy would be dedicated to God for life. The child's whole life was to be set apart for God's purpose.
entries.13:8: Manoah prayed and asked God to send the messenger again so they would know how to raise the child. It's a good example of a parent asking God for guidance.
entries.13:9: God listened to Manoah's prayer and the angel came to the woman again while she was alone in the field. God hears ordinary people's prayers and responds.
entries.13:10: The woman ran quickly to fetch her husband and told him the man from before had appeared again. She wanted her husband included in this important moment.
entries.13:11: Manoah followed his wife, asked the man if he was the one who had spoken to her, and the man said yes. Manoah took the news seriously enough to check it out himself.
entries.13:12: Manoah asked what the rules would be for the child and what his life's work would be. He wanted to know how to prepare for and raise this special son.
entries.13:13: The angel told Manoah that his wife should simply follow everything he had already told her. God's instructions were already clear enough to obey.
entries.13:14: She must avoid anything from the vine, wine or strong drink, and anything unclean, and do all he commanded. Obedience to God's specific directions mattered for the child's calling.
entries.13:15: Manoah offered to prepare a young goat so the visitor could stay and eat with them. He wanted to show hospitality to this mysterious messenger.
entries.13:16: The angel refused the food but said if they made a burnt offering it should go to the Lord, since Manoah didn't yet realize who he was. The honor belonged to God, not to the messenger.
entries.13:17: Manoah asked the angel's name so they could honor him when the promise came true. He wanted to give credit and respect to the one who brought the news.
entries.13:18: The angel said his name was beyond understanding, so there was no point asking. The messenger was pointing to something too wonderful for Manoah to grasp.
entries.13:19: Manoah offered the goat and grain offering on a rock to the Lord, who did something wonderful. Worship was the right response to this extraordinary encounter.
entries.13:20: As the flame rose from the altar, the angel went up in it while Manoah and his wife watched, and they fell face down. They realized they were in the presence of something far greater than themselves.
entries.13:21: The angel never appeared to them again, and then Manoah understood it really had been the angel of the Lord. The truth of who they had met finally sank in.
entries.13:22: Manoah panicked, thinking they would die because they had seen God. It was a common fear in that time, but his fear was mistaken.
entries.13:23: His wife reasoned that if God meant to kill them, he wouldn't have accepted their offering or given them these promises about a son. Her calm faith corrected his fear.
entries.13:24: The woman gave birth to a son and named him Samson, and he grew up with the Lord's blessing on him. God kept his promise, and the child grew under God's care.
entries.13:25: The Spirit of the Lord began to stir Samson at Mahaneh-dan, between Zorah and Eshtaol. God was starting to work through Samson for Israel's rescue.
entries.14:1: Samson traveled to a Philistine town and noticed a woman there. This sets up a choice that will cause trouble, showing how a strong person can still be led by what looks good to him.
entries.14:2: He went home and told his parents to arrange a marriage with this Philistine woman. He expected them to simply do what he wanted because he liked her.
entries.14:3: His parents objected, asking why he couldn't marry a woman from his own people instead of from a group they considered outsiders. Samson ignored their concerns and insisted, because he only cared that she pleased him.
entries.14:4: His parents didn't realize God was using this situation for his own plan against the Philistines, who were ruling over Israel at the time. Even when people make selfish choices, God can still work through them.
entries.14:5: Samson went down to Timnah with his parents and, near the vineyards, a young lion suddenly charged at him. Trouble came at him unexpectedly on an ordinary trip.
entries.14:6: God's Spirit gave Samson sudden strength, and he killed the lion with his bare hands. He kept it a secret from his parents, showing he was already keeping parts of his life hidden from them.
entries.14:7: He continued on and talked with the woman, and he still found her pleasing. His attraction to her remained strong even after the dangerous encounter.
entries.14:8: Later, on his way back to marry her, he turned aside to look at the lion's carcass and found bees and honey inside it. Something sweet had come from something dead and dangerous.
entries.14:9: He scooped up the honey, ate some as he walked, and shared it with his parents without telling them where it came from. He gave them a gift but kept the truth about it to himself.
entries.14:10: Samson went to the woman and held a wedding feast, as young men customarily did. This was a normal celebration that would soon turn into a contest.
entries.14:11: Thirty men were brought in to be with him at the feast. These companions would become the opponents in his riddle.
entries.14:12: Samson proposed a bet: if they could answer his riddle within the seven days of the feast, he would give them thirty sets of clothes. He turned the celebration into a challenge with a costly stake.
entries.14:13: He told them that if they couldn't solve it, they would owe him thirty sets of clothes instead. They agreed and asked to hear the riddle.
entries.14:14: His riddle described food coming from a eater and sweetness coming from something strong, pointing to the honey and the lion. After three days, they still had no answer.
entries.14:15: On the fourth day they threatened Samson's wife, saying they would burn her and her family if she didn't get the answer for them. They were willing to harm her to avoid losing the bet.
entries.14:16: His wife cried and accused him of not loving her because he wouldn't tell her the answer. He pointed out that he hadn't even told his own parents.
entries.14:17: She kept crying about it for the rest of the seven days, and finally he told her because she wouldn't let up. She then passed the answer on to her people.
entries.14:18: Before the wedding night, the men gave him the answer, revealing they had gotten it through his wife. Samson replied that they would never have solved it without using her to pressure him.
entries.14:19: God's Spirit gave Samson power again, and he went to another Philistine city, killed thirty men, and gave their clothes to the men who had answered. Furious, he went back to his father's house.
entries.14:20: Samson's wife was then given to one of the men who had been his companion at the wedding. His marriage ended in betrayal and loss.
entries.15:1: Samson went to visit his wife with a gift, expecting to go into her room, but her father blocked the door. It shows how their marriage was already broken by her family's actions.
entries.15:2: Her father assumed Samson hated her, so he had given her to another man and offered her younger sister instead. It shows how casually the father treated Samson's marriage.
entries.15:3: Samson declared that this time he was justified in harming the Philistines. He was shifting from personal anger to a deliberate act of revenge.
entries.15:4: Samson caught three hundred foxes and tied them in pairs with a torch between their tails. This was a clever and destructive plan aimed at the Philistines' crops.
entries.15:5: He set the torches on fire and let the animals run through the Philistines' fields, burning grain, vines, and olive trees. It was a devastating blow to their food and income.
entries.15:6: When the Philistines found out Samson did it because his wife was given to another man, they burned her and her father to death. Their cruelty shows how little they valued human life.
entries.15:7: Samson told them that since they had done this, he would take his revenge and then stop. He was drawing a line, though his anger was far from over.
entries.15:8: Samson attacked them fiercely and then went to hide in a rock cave at Etam. He had won a battle but was now a fugitive.
entries.15:9: The Philistines set up camp in Judah to go after Samson. Their presence put pressure on the people of Judah.
entries.15:10: The men of Judah asked why the Philistines had come, and they answered that they wanted Samson to pay for what he had done. The conflict was now spilling over onto Samson's own people.
entries.15:11: Three thousand men of Judah confronted Samson, reminding him that the Philistines ruled over them and asking what he had done. They were afraid of the consequences of his actions.
entries.15:12: The men of Judah told Samson they had come to hand him over to the Philistines. Samson asked them to promise not to attack him themselves.
entries.15:13: They agreed not to kill him but to tie him up and hand him over. They bound him with two new ropes and led him away from the rock.
entries.15:14: When the Philistines came shouting to meet him, the Spirit of the Lord came on Samson powerfully, and the ropes fell off his arms like burned grass. God gave him strength at the critical moment.
entries.15:15: Samson grabbed the fresh jawbone of a donkey lying nearby and used it to kill a thousand men. It shows his raw strength being used in battle.
entries.15:16: Samson boasted in a poem about using the jawbone to strike down a thousand men. He was celebrating his victory in a proud, vivid way.
entries.15:17: After his boast, he threw the jawbone away, and the place was named after it. The name marked the spot of his great victory.
entries.15:18: Exhausted and thirsty, Samson cried out to God, reminding him of the great victory and fearing he would die of thirst or fall into enemy hands. Even a strong man can be brought low by basic needs.
entries.15:19: God split open a hollow place in the rock, and water came out; after drinking, Samson revived. God answered his cry and gave him strength again.
entries.15:20: Samson led Israel as judge for twenty years during the time the Philistines were in power. His story shows God using an imperfect man to deliver his people.
entries.16:1: Samson went to a Philistine town and slept with a prostitute there. Even a man with great strength from God can make foolish and sinful choices, so we should be careful about what we let ourselves do.
entries.16:2: The people of Gaza found out Samson was in town and planned to kill him at dawn, so they waited quietly all day. People who want to harm you may seem calm while they plot, so it pays to be alert.
entries.16:3: Samson got up in the middle of the night, ripped the town gates out of the ground, and carried them to a hill far away. This shows his amazing strength, but it also shows he was treating a dangerous situation lightly.
entries.16:4: Later Samson fell in love with a woman named Delilah. Love can be a good thing, but it can also lead us into trouble if we give our heart to the wrong person.
entries.16:5: The Philistine rulers offered Delilah a huge amount of money to find out the secret of Samson's strength and how to capture him. People will sometimes pay a high price to bring someone down, so be careful who you trust with your secrets.
entries.16:6: Delilah asked Samson straight out what made him so strong and how he could be tied up. When someone asks about your weaknesses right after being offered money, that is a warning sign.
entries.16:7: Samson gave her a false answer, saying fresh bowstrings would make him weak. He was playing a game with her instead of being honest, and that game would cost him dearly.
entries.16:8: The Philistine rulers brought the bowstrings to Delilah, and she tied Samson up with them. The trap was being set exactly as she planned, and Samson let it happen.
entries.16:9: Men were hiding in the room, and when Delilah shouted that the Philistines were coming, Samson snapped the cords like thread. His strength was still with him, but he did not seem to realize how dangerous this game was.
entries.16:10: Delilah complained that Samson had lied to her and demanded the real answer. She kept pressing him, and he kept making up stories instead of walking away.
