entries.16:11: Samson gave another false answer, saying new unused ropes would make him weak. He was still toying with her, not taking seriously the danger he was in.
entries.16:12: Delilah tied him with new ropes, and again men were hiding nearby, and again Samson broke free. The pattern repeated, and Samson kept ignoring the warning signs.
entries.16:13: Delilah complained again and asked for the truth, and Samson gave a third false answer about weaving his hair into cloth. He was getting closer to the truth but still not honest.
entries.16:14: While Samson slept, Delilah wove his hair into the cloth and pinned it, then shouted that the Philistines were coming, and he pulled it all loose. He was sleeping through a trap that was closing in on him.
entries.16:15: Delilah accused Samson of not really loving her because he kept his secret from her. This is a common way to pressure someone, and Samson was starting to give in.
entries.16:16: She nagged him day after day until he was worn out and miserable. Constant pressure can wear down even a strong person, so we should be aware of people who won't let us alone.
entries.16:17: Samson finally told her the truth: his hair had never been cut because he was set apart to God from birth, and cutting it would take away his strength. He gave away the one thing that marked him as God's special servant.
entries.16:18: Delilah saw he had finally told the truth, so she called the Philistine rulers to come with the money. She had gotten what she wanted, and Samson had handed her the key to his downfall.
entries.16:19: Delilah put Samson to sleep on her lap and had his hair cut off, and his strength left him. The very thing that set him apart for God was taken from him while he slept.
entries.16:20: Samson woke up and thought he could shake himself free as before, not realizing the Lord had left him. We can get so used to God's help that we stop noticing when it is gone.
entries.16:21: The Philistines captured Samson, blinded him, chained him in bronze, and made him grind grain in prison. His foolish choices led to terrible suffering, a sober warning about the cost of sin.
entries.16:22: Even in prison, Samson's hair began to grow back. God had not completely abandoned him, and there was still hope for what would come next.
entries.16:23: The Philistine rulers gathered to offer a great sacrifice to their god Dagon and celebrate, saying their god had handed Samson over to them. They gave credit to a false god for what had happened.
entries.16:24: When the people saw Samson, they praised their god for giving them victory over the man who had fought against them and killed many of them. People often celebrate a victory without understanding the real story behind it.
entries.16:25: While everyone was celebrating, they brought Samson out of prison to entertain them, and he stood between the pillars of the building. He was being mocked and humiliated in front of his enemies.
entries.16:26: Samson asked the boy leading him to let him lean his hands on the pillars that held up the building. Even blind and weak, he was thinking about what he could do.
entries.16:27: The building was packed with men and women, including all the Philistine rulers, and about three thousand more were on the roof watching Samson. A huge crowd had gathered to laugh at him.
entries.16:28: Samson prayed and asked God to remember him and give him strength one more time, so he could pay back the Philistines for his eyes. Even after all his failures, he turned to God in his last moment.
entries.16:29: Samson put his arms around the two middle pillars that held up the building, leaning on them with his right and left hands. He was positioning himself to bring the whole structure down.
entries.16:30: Samson asked to die with the Philistines, then pushed with all his strength and the building collapsed on everyone, killing more in his death than he had killed in his life. God answered his prayer, but it cost him his own life.
entries.16:31: Samson's family came and buried him in his father's tomb, and he had judged Israel for twenty years. His story ends with both his failures and God's mercy, a reminder that God can still use flawed people.
entries.17:1: This introduces Micah, a man from the hill country of Ephraim. The story that follows shows how people were living by their own ideas rather than God's.
entries.17:2: Micah confesses to his mother that he stole her large amount of silver, and she responds with a blessing instead of anger. It shows how even within a family, right and wrong were being handled loosely.
entries.17:3: His mother dedicates the returned silver to the Lord, but her plan is to use it to make carved idols. She means well in her own eyes, yet she is mixing worship of God with forbidden images.
entries.17:4: She gives part of the silver to a craftsman who makes an idol, which ends up in Micah's house. Money set apart for God is being used to make something God had clearly forbidden.
entries.17:5: Micah sets up his own shrine with idols, a priestly garment, and household gods, and he installs one of his sons as priest. He is inventing his own religion instead of following what God commanded.
entries.17:6: This explains why all this happened: there was no king, so everyone did whatever seemed right to themselves. It warns that when people ignore God's standards, they end up living by their own opinions.
entries.17:7: A young Levite from Bethlehem in Judah is introduced; Levites were supposed to serve in God's worship. He is away from home and looking for a place to settle.
entries.17:8: The Levite leaves Bethlehem to find a place to live and arrives at Micah's house in the hill country of Ephraim. He is simply looking for a livelihood, not for God's direction.
entries.17:9: Micah asks where he is from, and the young man explains he is a Levite from Bethlehem looking for somewhere to stay. His answer sets up the offer that follows.
entries.17:10: Micah offers the Levite a paid position as his personal priest, with wages, clothes, and food. He treats a sacred role like a job he can hire someone to fill.
entries.17:11: The Levite agrees to stay with Micah and becomes like a son to him. He accepts the arrangement even though it means serving at a shrine full of idols.
entries.17:12: Micah officially installs the Levite as his priest in his house. This shows how far things had drifted, since a Levite was now serving a private idol shrine.
entries.17:13: Micah is confident God will bless him simply because he has a Levite as his priest. He trusts in the outward arrangement rather than in genuine obedience to God.
entries.18:1: At this time Israel had no king, so everyone did what seemed right to them. The tribe of Dan still had no land of their own to settle in, so they went looking for a place to live.
entries.18:2: The Danites sent five brave men to explore the land and find a good place. On their journey they stopped for the night at Micah's house in the hill country of Ephraim.
entries.18:3: The men recognized the voice of the young Levite and were curious about him. They stopped to ask how he ended up living there.
entries.18:4: The Levite explained that Micah had hired him and paid him to serve as his personal priest.
entries.18:5: The men asked the priest to ask God whether their journey would succeed.
entries.18:6: The priest told them to go in peace and said the Lord would guide their way.
entries.18:7: The five men came to Laish and found a people living carelessly and feeling safe, with plenty of everything and no nearby allies to protect them.
entries.18:8: The men returned home to their fellow Danites, who asked them what they had found.
entries.18:9: The spies urged their people to attack Laish right away, saying the land was excellent and there was no reason to delay.
entries.18:10: They described a people who felt safe and a wide, rich land that God had put within their reach.
entries.18:11: So six hundred Danite men from Zorah and Eshtaol set out ready for battle.
entries.18:12: They camped near Kiriath-jearim in Judah, and the place was called Mahaneh-dan, meaning Dan's camp, from that day on.
entries.18:13: From there they traveled into the hill country of Ephraim and arrived at Micah's house.
entries.18:14: The five spies reminded their companions that Micah's house held religious objects, including an ephod and idols, and hinted they should take them.
entries.18:15: The men turned aside to Micah's house and greeted the young Levite, asking if all was well with him.
entries.18:16: The six hundred armed Danites stood guard at the entrance of the house.
entries.18:17: The five spies went inside and took the idols and the ephod while the priest stood at the door with the armed men.
entries.18:18: When the men came out carrying Micah's religious objects, the priest asked them what they were doing.
entries.18:19: They told him to be quiet and come with them, arguing it was better to be priest for a whole tribe than for one man's household.
entries.18:20: The priest was pleased with this offer, so he took the religious objects and joined the Danites.
entries.18:21: The Danites continued on their way, placing their children, livestock, and possessions in front for safety.
entries.18:22: After they had traveled some distance from Micah's house, Micah and his neighbors caught up with them.
entries.18:23: The Danites turned and asked Micah why he had gathered men and come after them.
entries.18:24: Micah said they had taken his gods and his priest, leaving him with nothing, so he had good reason to be upset.
entries.18:25: The Danites warned Micah to stop complaining, or angry men might attack and kill him and his people.
entries.18:26: The Danites went on their way, and Micah, seeing they were too strong for him, turned back home.
entries.18:27: The Danites took Micah's idols and his priest, then attacked the peaceful people of Laish with the sword and burned their town.
entries.18:28: No one came to help Laish because it was far from Sidon and had no allies, so the Danites rebuilt the town and settled there.
entries.18:29: They renamed the town Dan after their ancestor Dan, son of Israel, though it had formerly been called Laish.
entries.18:30: The Danites set up the carved image for themselves, and Jonathan, a descendant of Moses, and his sons served as priests for the tribe of Dan until the ark was captured.
entries.18:31: They kept Micah's carved image set up for themselves the whole time God's house was at Shiloh.
entries.19:1: This sets the scene in a time when Israel had no king, so everyone did as they pleased. It introduces a Levite and his concubine, and the lack of leadership hints that trouble is coming.
entries.19:2: The woman was unfaithful to him and left to stay with her father for four months. Her leaving sets off the chain of events that follows.
entries.19:3: Her husband went to win her back and speak kindly to her, bringing supplies and a servant. Her father welcomed him warmly, showing the man meant to make peace.
entries.19:4: His father-in-law urged him to stay three days, and they ate, drank, and rested together. The hospitality was generous and relaxed.
entries.19:5: On the fourth day the man tried to leave early, but his father-in-law pressed him to eat first for strength. The repeated delays show how much the father wanted him to stay.
entries.19:6: They sat down to eat and drink together, and the father-in-law invited him to stay another night and enjoy himself. The man's plans to leave kept getting pushed back.
entries.19:7: The man got up to go, but his father-in-law persuaded him to stay one more night. The pressure to linger was strong.
entries.19:8: On the fifth day the man tried again, but the father-in-law urged him to eat, and they did not leave until midday. The delays were wearing on, and the day was slipping away.
entries.19:9: The father-in-law pointed out that evening was near and urged one more night's rest before an early start. He kept finding reasons for them to stay.
entries.19:10: This time the man refused to stay and left with his concubine and donkeys, heading toward Jebus (Jerusalem). His decision to leave late set them up to be on the road at nightfall.
entries.19:11: As they neared Jebus, the servant suggested stopping there for the night. It seemed like a sensible plan.
entries.19:12: The master refused to stay in a non-Israelite town and insisted on going on to Gibeah. His choice of where to stop would prove fateful.
entries.19:13: He suggested they press on to Gibeah or Ramah to spend the night. They kept moving as darkness came.
entries.19:14: They continued and reached the area of Gibeah in Benjamin's territory just as the sun set. They were now far from home with night falling.
entries.19:15: They stopped in Gibeah and sat in the town square, but no one offered them a place to stay. Being left outside at night was a sign of danger and cold hospitality.
entries.19:16: An old man from Ephraim, living among the Benjamites, came in from his field and saw them. He was an outsider in that town, which may explain his kindness.
entries.19:17: The old man asked the traveler where he was going and where he came from. A simple question opened the way for hospitality.
entries.19:18: The man explained he was traveling home from Bethlehem to Ephraim and that no one would take him in. His words show he was a stranger with nowhere to go.
entries.19:19: He assured the old man they had everything they needed for themselves and their animals. They were not asking for supplies, only shelter.
entries.19:20: The old man welcomed him and promised to take care of all his needs, insisting he not sleep in the street. This was the kindness the traveler had been waiting for.
entries.19:21: He brought them into his house, fed the donkeys, washed their feet, and gave them food and drink. The old man showed full hospitality.
entries.19:22: While they were enjoying the meal, worthless men of the town surrounded the house and pounded on the door, demanding the guest be sent out so they could abuse him. The scene turns from welcome to terror.
entries.19:23: The old man went out and pleaded with them not to do this wicked thing, reminding them the man was his guest. He tried to protect him.
entries.19:24: In a shocking offer, the old man proposed sending out his virgin daughter and the man's concubine instead, begging them not to shame his guest. This shows how badly women were treated in that culture.
entries.19:25: The men refused to listen, so the man pushed his concubine out to them, and they abused her all night until morning. This is a horrifying act of cruelty and betrayal.
entries.19:26: At dawn the woman crawled back to the door of the house where her master was and collapsed there until daylight. She had nowhere else to go and was left broken.
entries.19:27: In the morning her master got up to leave and found her lying at the door with her hands on the threshold. He expected to find her ready to travel.
entries.19:28: He told her to get up so they could go, but she did not answer, so he put her on the donkey and went home. The text leaves it unclear whether she was dead or unconscious.
entries.19:29: At home he cut her body into twelve pieces and sent them throughout Israel. This gruesome act was meant to shock the nation into responding to the crime.
entries.19:30: He told the messengers to ask all Israel whether such a thing had ever happened since they left Egypt, and to consider what should be done. The question demanded a response to the horror, and the story shows how far Israel had fallen without good leadership.
entries.20:1: The whole nation gathered as one united army, from the far north to the far south and from the east too, and they met in the Lord's presence. It shows how seriously they treated this crisis and that they wanted God involved.
entries.20:2: The leaders of every tribe took their places before God with a huge fighting force of four hundred thousand swordsmen. The point is that this was a national, organized response, not a small quarrel.
entries.20:3: Benjamin heard that the rest of Israel had gathered, and the others asked for a full account of what had happened. They wanted the facts before deciding what to do.
entries.20:4: The Levite, whose wife had died, told his side of the story: he had come to Gibeah in Benjamin's territory just to spend the night. He was a traveler seeking shelter, not looking for trouble.
entries.20:5: He explained that the men of the town surrounded the house at night intending to kill him, and they abused his wife so badly that she died. This was the crime that sparked the whole gathering.
entries.20:6: He had cut her body into pieces and sent them throughout Israel to shock the nation into action, because such a terrible thing had been done. He was appealing to them to respond to a grave injustice.
entries.20:7: He turned the decision over to the assembled Israelites, asking them to decide what should be done. The responsibility for justice now rested with the whole community.
entries.20:8: The people responded with total unity, saying none of them would go home until the matter was settled. They were determined not to ignore the crime.
entries.20:9: They agreed on a plan to march against Gibeah, believing their decision was in line with the Lord's will. They moved from outrage to organized action.
entries.20:10: They arranged for a small share of men from each tribe to supply food for the army, so the rest could carry out the deserved punishment on Gibeah. It shows careful planning and shared responsibility.
entries.20:11: All the men of Israel came together against the town as a single united force. The nation was completely of one mind about confronting this evil.
entries.20:12: Before attacking, the tribes sent messengers throughout Benjamin asking them to explain the evil done among them. They gave Benjamin a chance to answer and take responsibility.
entries.20:13: Israel demanded that the guilty men of Gibeah be handed over to be executed so the evil could be removed from the nation. Benjamin refused to listen to their fellow Israelites, choosing to protect the offenders.
entries.20:14: Instead of handing over the guilty, the Benjamites gathered from all their towns to fight against the rest of Israel. They sided with the wrongdoers rather than with justice.
entries.20:15: Benjamin mustered twenty-six thousand swordsmen from their towns, plus seven hundred specially chosen fighters from Gibeah. Though far outnumbered, they prepared for war.
entries.20:16: Among them were seven hundred left-handed men who could sling a stone at a hair and never miss. These were highly skilled, deadly accurate fighters.
entries.20:17: Israel, apart from Benjamin, counted four hundred thousand swordsmen, all experienced soldiers. The odds heavily favored Israel's side.
entries.20:18: Before fighting, Israel went to Bethel to ask God who should lead the attack, and God answered that Judah should go first. They sought God's direction before acting.
entries.20:19: Israel rose early and took up battle positions against Gibeah. They were ready to carry out the attack they had planned.
entries.20:20: The men of Israel advanced and drew up their battle lines against Benjamin at Gibeah. The fighting was about to begin.
entries.20:21: Benjamin came out and killed twenty-two thousand Israelites that day. Despite being right about the cause, Israel suffered a devastating defeat.
entries.20:22: The Israelite army encouraged each other and took up the same battle position as the first day. They refused to give up after the loss.
entries.20:23: Israel wept before the Lord until evening, asking whether they should fight their brother Benjamin again, and the Lord told them to go up. They sought God's will even in their grief.
entries.20:24: Israel advanced against Benjamin a second time. They obeyed what they believed God had told them.
entries.20:25: Benjamin again came out from Gibeah and killed eighteen thousand Israelite swordsmen. The second day brought another terrible loss.
entries.20:26: All Israel went up to Bethel, wept, fasted all day until evening, and offered burnt and peace offerings to the Lord. They humbled themselves before God after two defeats.
entries.20:27: Israel asked the Lord for guidance, and the ark of God's covenant was there in those days. They wanted God's direct answer before continuing.
entries.20:28: Phinehas, grandson of Aaron, served before the ark, and Israel asked whether to keep fighting Benjamin or stop. The Lord said to go on, promising victory the next day.
entries.20:29: Israel set men in hiding all around Gibeah to launch a surprise attack. They combined seeking God with careful military strategy.
entries.20:30: On the third day Israel went up and arranged their battle lines against Gibeah as before. They followed the plan God had approved.
entries.20:31: Benjamin came out and killed about thirty Israelites on the roads and in the open country, just as in earlier fights. They thought they were winning again.
entries.20:32: Benjamin thought Israel was retreating as before, but Israel was deliberately pulling back to draw them away from the town. It was a trap.
entries.20:33: Israel took their battle position at Baal-tamar, and the men hidden in ambush rushed out from their place west of Geba. The trap was sprung.
entries.20:34: Ten thousand of Israel's best men attacked in front of Gibeah, and the fighting grew fierce, but Benjamin did not realize disaster was coming. They were blind to the danger closing in.
entries.20:35: The Lord threw Benjamin into panic before Israel, and Israel killed twenty-five thousand one hundred Benjamite swordsmen that day. God gave the victory Israel had been promised.
entries.20:36: Benjamin finally saw they were beaten; Israel had deliberately given ground, trusting the men hidden in ambush against Gibeah. The retreat had been part of the plan all along.
entries.20:37: The hidden men rushed into Gibeah, captured it, and put the whole town to the sword without mercy. The ambush succeeded completely.
entries.20:38: Israel and the ambush party had agreed on a signal: a column of smoke rising from the town. This would tell the main army when the town had been taken.
entries.20:39: At that point Israel was to turn back and fight; Benjamin had killed about thirty men and thought Israel was retreating as before. Benjamin was still fooled by the trap.
entries.20:40: Then the smoke signal rose from the town, and the Benjamites looked back and saw the whole city going up in smoke. They realized too late that they had been defeated.
entries.20:41: The Israelites had tricked the Benjaminites by circling back, and suddenly the Benjaminites realized they were trapped and doomed. It shows how quickly a situation can turn when you think you are winning.
entries.20:42: The Benjaminites ran toward the desert to escape, but the fighting caught up with them and other Israelites came out of the town to cut them off. There was no safe way out for them.
entries.20:43: The Israelites surrounded and crushed the Benjaminites, chasing them from Nohah toward the east of Gibeah. The pursuit was relentless and gave them no rest.
entries.20:44: Eighteen thousand of Benjamin's best soldiers died in that battle. The loss was enormous for a small tribe.
entries.20:45: The survivors fled toward a rocky place called Rimmon, but the Israelites caught and killed five thousand along the roads and two thousand more near Geba. Even the escape route became a place of death.
entries.20:46: In total, twenty-five thousand Benjaminite soldiers died that day. It was a devastating defeat that nearly wiped out the tribe's fighting force.
entries.20:47: Only six hundred men survived by hiding at the rock of Rimmon, where they stayed for four months. A whole tribe was reduced to a small remnant hiding in fear.
entries.20:48: The Israelites then went through Benjamin's towns, killing people and animals and burning everything. The punishment went far beyond the battlefield and left the tribe's homeland in ruins.
entries.21:1: The Israelites had sworn a solemn promise not to let their daughters marry any man from the tribe of Benjamin. That oath later trapped them, because it left Benjamin with no way to keep its families going.
entries.21:2: The people went to Bethel and sat crying bitterly before God until evening. Their grief shows how deeply the near-destruction of one tribe hurt the whole nation.
entries.21:3: They asked God why Israel had come to this point, with one whole tribe now missing. They were bewildered that such a loss had happened among God's own people.
entries.21:4: Early the next day they built an altar and offered sacrifices to God. They were turning to worship while still trying to deal with the damage they had caused.
entries.21:5: They asked who had failed to show up at the national gathering, because they had sworn to put to death anyone who stayed away. That oath set up the next tragic step.
entries.21:6: The Israelites felt sorry for Benjamin, their fellow tribe, and grieved that one tribe had been lost from Israel. Their pity shows they knew something precious had been nearly wiped out.
entries.21:7: They were stuck: the surviving Benjaminite men needed wives, but the Israelites had sworn not to give them their own daughters. Their own promise now stood in the way of fixing the problem.
entries.21:8: They checked which tribe had not come to the gathering at Mizpah, and found that no one from Jabesh-gilead had shown up. That discovery gave them a way to find wives without breaking their oath.
entries.21:9: When the people were counted, none of Jabesh-gilead was there. Their absence made them the target of the oath's penalty.
entries.21:10: The assembly sent twelve thousand fighting men with orders to kill everyone in Jabesh-gilead, including women and children. This was a brutal act done to solve a problem the Israelites had created themselves.
entries.21:11: They were told to kill every male and every woman who had been with a man, but to spare the virgins. The command treated the young women as survivors to be taken.
entries.21:12: They found four hundred young women who had never been with a man and brought them to the camp at Shiloh. These women were taken to become wives for the surviving Benjaminites.
entries.21:13: The whole assembly sent word to the Benjaminite men hiding at the rock of Rimmon, offering them peace. They were trying to bring the surviving tribe back into the nation.
entries.21:14: Benjamin came back, and the four hundred women from Jabesh-gilead were given to them as wives. But there were still not enough women for all the men.
entries.21:15: The people felt sorry for Benjamin because the Lord had allowed disaster to fall on the tribes of Israel. Their pity came after great violence had already been done.
entries.21:16: The leaders asked what could be done for the remaining Benjaminite men, since the women of Benjamin were dead. They still needed a way to keep the tribe from dying out.
entries.21:17: They wanted the survivors of Benjamin to have children so the tribe would not disappear from Israel. Keeping the tribe alive had become their main concern.
entries.21:18: They could not give their own daughters to Benjamin because of the oath they had sworn. So they looked for another way around their promise.
entries.21:19: They pointed out that a yearly festival of the Lord was held at Shiloh, and they described where it was located. That festival would become the setting for their plan.
entries.21:20: They told the Benjaminite men to hide in the vineyards. This was the start of a scheme to get wives without formally breaking the oath.
entries.21:21: They were to watch for the young women of Shiloh coming out to dance, then seize one each and take her home to Benjamin. The plan used force and surprise rather than a proper marriage arrangement.
entries.21:22: If the women's fathers or brothers complained, the leaders would ask them to let it go, arguing that the men had not been given wives in war and that the families would not be guilty of breaking the oath. This was a convenient excuse to cover the wrongdoing.
entries.21:23: The Benjaminites did as told, each grabbing a wife from the dancers, then returned to rebuild their towns and settle there. The tribe survived, but through kidnapping rather than honorable means.
entries.21:24: The Israelites then went home, each to his own tribe and family and inherited land. The national crisis ended and everyone returned to normal life.
entries.21:25: There was no king in Israel at that time, and everyone did whatever seemed right to himself. This explains why so much confusion and wrongdoing happened, and it warns against a life guided only by personal opinion.
